questions.question: How do Reformed and Eastern Orthodox views of tradition and authority differ?
questions.reference_answer: Must contrast Sola Scriptura (Reformed) with Sacred Tradition as a co-equal source of authority (EO). Should address the role of ecumenical councils, church fathers, and the relationship between Scripture and tradition.

scoring.rubric: Must contrast Sola Scriptura (Reformed) with Sacred Tradition as a co-equal source of authority (EO). Should address the role of ecumenical councils, church fathers, and the relationship between Scripture and tradition.

questions.response:
The **Reformed** (Calvinist) and **Eastern Orthodox** traditions differ significantly in their views on **tradition** and **authority**, particularly in how they understand the relationship between Scripture, the Church, and historical development. Below is a comparison of their key differences:

---

### **1. Source of Authority**
| **Aspect**            | **Reformed (Calvinist) View** | **Eastern Orthodox View** |
|-----------------------|-----------------------------|--------------------------|
| **Ultimate Authority** | **Sola Scriptura** – Scripture alone is the supreme and final authority in matters of faith and practice. | **Holy Tradition** – Scripture is part of a broader, divinely inspired Tradition that includes the Church’s liturgy, councils, Fathers, and lived experience. |
| **Role of Scripture** | Scripture is **self-authenticating** (2 Tim. 3:16-17) and **perspicuous** (clear in essentials). Tradition is subordinate and must be tested by Scripture. | Scripture is **within Tradition**—it was formed by the Church and must be interpreted **within** the Church’s living Tradition. |
| **Role of the Church** | The Church is **a created means** to proclaim and guard Scripture, but it has no infallible authority apart from Scripture. | The Church is **the pillar and ground of the truth** (1 Tim. 3:15) and **infallible in its collective life** (though not in individual members). |

---

### **2. Understanding of Tradition**
| **Aspect**            | **Reformed View** | **Eastern Orthodox View** |
|-----------------------|------------------|--------------------------|
| **Definition of Tradition** | **Historical tradition** – Human traditions (e.g., creeds, confessions) are useful but **fallible** and must be judged by Scripture. | **Holy Tradition (Ἁγία Παραδοσις)** – The **living, unbroken continuity** of the Church’s faith, including Scripture, ecumenical councils, liturgy, icons, and the consensus of the Fathers. It is **divinely guided** and **infallible** in its essence. |
| **Development of Doctrine** | **No new revelation** – Doctrine may be **clarified** but not **developed** beyond Scripture. The Reformation was a **return** to pure Scripture. | **Organic development** – Doctrine unfolds over time under the Holy Spirit’s guidance (e.g., Trinitarian and Christological definitions at councils). The Church **discerns** truth, not invents it. |
| **Creeds & Councils** | **Useful but not infallible** – Confessions (e.g., Westminster, Heidelberg) are human summaries of Scripture. Ecumenical creeds (Nicene, Chalcedon) are **highly respected** but not **binding** in the same way as Scripture. | **Infallible when received by the whole Church** – The **Seven Ecumenical Councils** are **binding** because they express the **mind of the Church** under the Spirit’s guidance. |
| **Patristic Writings** | **Helpful but not authoritative** – The Fathers are respected but **not infallible**; their teachings must align with Scripture. | **Authoritative as part of Tradition** – The **consensus of the Fathers** (especially those of the first 5-7 centuries) is a **normative guide** for interpreting Scripture. |

---

### **3. Ecclesiology (Church Authority)**
| **Aspect**            | **Reformed View** | **Eastern Orthodox View** |
|-----------------------|------------------|--------------------------|
| **Church Governance** | **Presbyterian/Reformed** – Rule by elders (presbyters) in a **conciliar** but **non-hierarchical** structure (e.g., synods). Some Reformed churches have bishops, but they have no **sacramental** or **infallible** authority. | **Episcopal & Conciliar** – Bishops are successors of the Apostles, with **real authority** in teaching and governance. **Autocephalous** (self-governing) churches are united in **conciliarity** (sobornost). |
| **Infallibility** | **No infallible church authority** – Only Scripture is inerrant. The Church can err and has erred (e.g., Roman Catholicism, medieval corruptions). | **The Church as a whole is infallible** – Not in the sense of a single pope, but in the **consensus of the faithful** (sensus fidelium) and the **reception** of councils by the whole Church. |
| **Sacraments & Apostolic Succession** | **Sacraments are signs and seals** of God’s covenant, but their efficacy depends on **faith**, not on apostolic succession. Ordination is **not** a sacrament in most Reformed views. | **Sacraments are efficacious by the Holy Spirit** and require **apostolic succession** (bishops tracing back to the Apostles) for validity. The Eucharist is the **true Body and Blood of Christ** (though not in a forensic, Western sense). |

---

### **4. Hermeneutics (Interpretation of Scripture)**
| **Aspect**            | **Reformed View** | **Eastern Orthodox View** |
|-----------------------|------------------|--------------------------|
| **Who Interprets Scripture?** | **Every believer (priesthood of all believers)** – The Holy Spirit illumines individuals, but **private interpretation** is subject to **Scripture’s clarity** and **sound exegesis**. | **The Church interprets Scripture** – Individual reading is valid, but **true understanding** comes through the **living Tradition** of the Church. |
| **Role of Reason & History** | **Historical-grammatical method** – Scripture is interpreted in its **original context**, with reason aiding understanding. | **Patristic & Liturgical Interpretation** – Scripture is read **allegorically, morally, and anagogically** (fourfold sense) as well as literally, always in light of **worship and the Fathers**. |
| **Sola Scriptura vs. Tradition** | **Scripture judges Tradition** – If a tradition (e.g., papal supremacy, purgatory) contradicts Scripture, it must be rejected. | **Tradition judges interpretations** – If an interpretation contradicts the **consensus of the Church**, it is rejected (e.g., Nestorianism, Iconoclasm). |

---

### **5. Practical Implications**
| **Issue** | **Reformed Position** | **Eastern Orthodox Position** |
|-----------|----------------------|-----------------------------|
| **Icons & Images** | **Rejected (in most cases)** – The Second Commandment (Ex. 20:4-5) forbids images in worship. Some Reformed allow **non-devotional** art. | **Affirmed** – Icons are **windows to heaven**, not idols. The **Seventh Ecumenical Council (787)** defended their veneration. |
| **Liturgy & Worship** | **Regulative Principle** – Only what Scripture commands is permitted in worship (e.g., preaching, sacraments, prayer). | **Liturgical Tradition** – The Divine Liturgy (e.g., St. John Chrysostom’s) is **apostolic in origin** and **unchangeable in essence**. |
| **Theosis (Deification)** | **Sanctification** – Believers grow in holiness but **do not become divine** (a strict Creator-creature distinction). | **Theosis** – Humans are **called to participate in the divine nature** (2 Pet. 1:4) through union with Christ. |
| **Marian Theology** | **Rejects veneration of Mary** – She is a **model of faith** but not a **mediatrix** or **perpetual virgin** (some Reformed accept her virginity at Jesus’ birth but not afterward). | **Honors Mary as Theotokos** – She is **ever-virgin**, **panagia** (all-holy), and **intercessor**, but **not divine** and **not worshipped**. |
| **Church Unity** | **Denominationalism accepted** – True unity is **spiritual**, not institutional. Different Reformed churches may have varying practices. | **Visible Unity Required** – Schism is a **sin**; the Church is **one, holy, catholic, and apostolic** in a **visible** sense. |

---

### **Key Theological Differences Summary**
| **Topic** | **Reformed** | **Eastern Orthodox** |
|-----------|-------------|----------------------|
| **Authority** | Sola Scriptura | Scripture + Holy Tradition |
| **Infallibility** | Scripture alone | The Church in its fullness |
| **Tradition** | Fallible, subordinate to Scripture | Infallible, includes Scripture |
| **Councils** | Helpful but not binding | Ecumenical Councils are binding |
| **Church Government** | Presbyterian/Reformed (elder-led) | Episcopal (bishop-led, conciliar) |
| **Sacraments** | Signs and seals of grace | Mysteries (efficacious by the Spirit) |
| **Interpretation** | Individual + community, but Scripture is clear | Church-guided, patristic consensus |
